location.section: D828 ff. 1b.2-2b.7 (chapter 1, gleng gzhi'i le'u)

paraphrase: The setting: in Akaniṣṭha — the sky-expanse of dharmatā, the abode of mind itself, a palace of wisdom without obscuration — the all-creating king bodhicitta brings forth retinues from its own nature, its own essence and its own compassion: a dharmakāya retinue; sambhogakāya retinues called earth, water, fire, wind and space; emanation retinues of the beings of the desire, form and formless realms; and four kinds of yogins. None is separate from its nature, essence and compassion. The chapter closes: teacher, teaching, retinue, place and time arise from me and are primordially a single sphere (thig le).
speaker: the all-creating king, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po)
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

location.section: D828 ff. 2b.7-3b.7 (chapter 2)

paraphrase: Asked what purpose the five causes and five wisdom-bodies serve, the all-creating king answers that there is no maker apart from itself: it sets out the three teachers, the retinues and dharmatā. Its nature has three aspects and is bodhicitta: 'byang' (purified) as the three excellences purified in dharmatā, 'chub' (pervading) as pervading everything like space, 'sems' (mind) as the unceasing all-maker that makes everything into bodhicitta.
speaker: the all-creating king, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po)
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

location.section: D828 ff. 5a.6-6a.4 (chapter 4)

original.text: nga ni ye nas rang 'byung ye shes te/ /nga ni ye nas chos kun snying po yin/ /nga ni kun byed rgyal po byang chub sems/ /nga yi mtshan 'di sems dpa' rtogs par gyis/
original.edition: Derge Kangyur (sde dge bka' 'gyur), digital edition by Esukhia and Barom Theksum Choling, Tōh 828; Wylie by the unit (pyewts)
original.licence: Public domain (Derge xylograph; Esukhia/Barom digital edition, per the repository)

paraphrase: The all-creating king explains its names: 'I am primordially self-arising wisdom; I am the heart of all phenomena; I am the all-creating king, bodhicitta — understand my name and you understand all phenomena.' 'Self-arising' means without causes and conditions, beyond effort; 'wisdom' means unceasing and unobscured, revealing everything; 'byang' means primordially pure; 'chub' means pervading appearance and existence, vessel and contents, the buddhas of the three times and the beings of the six classes; 'sems' means entering and mastering all. Whoever knows its nature knows all teachers and teachings and is beyond action, effort and accomplishment, spontaneously present.
speaker: the all-creating king, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po)
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

location.section: D828 ff. 12b.1-14b.5 (chapter 9, gol sgrib skyon sel)

paraphrase: On deviations and obscurations: all appearances are of the essence of bodhicitta; ignorance and not-knowing are called the two obscurations, and seeking and accomplishing are called deviations. To conceive what is one's own as other is to obscure oneself by oneself. Rest happily in non-conceptual evenness: the ten great natures need no effort, and when they are not sought the three hundred and sixty deviations and obscurations have no place.
speaker: the all-creating king, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po)
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

location.section: D828 ff. 14b.5-18a.7 (chapter 10)

paraphrase: The three jewels are the all-creator's body, speech and mind; as teacher it makes the three kāyas, which set out the teaching as outer, inner and secret, each threefold, making nine: by nine passes, nine scriptures and nine paths one travels to the single vehicle, the all-creator's ground of awakening — yet the all-creator, beyond action and effort, arrives at the ground of awakening without travelling.
speaker: the all-creating king, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po)
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked). An early statement of a ninefold ordering culminating in the single vehicle; whether these nine are the nine vehicles of the later doxographies is the unit's reading (interpretation).

location.section: D828 ff. 21b.7-22a.7 (chapter 14, skal med la gsang ba'i le'u)

paraphrase: Why the nature is kept secret from the unfortunate: were the all-creator's nature taught openly to all, the three kāyas and the three teachers would lose their distinct teachings and vehicles, and nothing could be called 'excellent'; therefore the all-creating king teaches its own nature to itself, has not given this transmission to the teachers and retinues that arose from it, and it is to be shown to the Atiyoga yogin, who is the all-creator.
speaker: the all-creating king, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po)
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked). The chain of reasoning in this chapter is compressed; paraphrase low confidence.

location.section: D828 f. 38b.4-5 (chapter 31, rdo rje tshig drug gi le'u)

original.text: sna tshogs rang bzhin mi gnyis kyang / /cha shas nyid du spros dang bral/ /ji bzhin pa zhes mi rtog kyang / /rnam par snang mdzad kun du bzang / /zin pas rtsol ba'i nad spangs te/ /lhun gyis gnas pas gzhag pa yin/
original.edition: Derge Kangyur (sde dge bka' 'gyur), digital edition by Esukhia and Barom Theksum Choling, Tōh 828; Wylie by the unit (pyewts)
original.licence: Public domain (Derge xylograph; Esukhia/Barom digital edition, per the repository)

paraphrase: The six vajra lines: 'The nature of variety is non-dual; in its particulars it is free of elaboration. Though it is not conceived as "just so", Vairocana, the all-good, appears everywhere. Since it is already complete, abandon the sickness of effort; remaining spontaneously present is the settling.'
speaker: the all-creating king, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po)
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

original.text: kye sems dpa' chen po 'di ltar don rig gis/ /ji ltar snang ba de bzhin nyid du gcig /'di la su yang 'chos par ma byed cig /ma bcos mnyam pa'i rgyal po de la ni/ /mi rtog chos sku'i dgongs pa de la gnas/

paraphrase: The four lines of certainty: 'O great being, know the meaning thus: however things appear, they are one in suchness. Let no one alter this. In that king of unaltered evenness, abide in the non-conceptual intention of the dharmakāya.'
speaker: the all-creating king, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po)

location.section: D828 ff. 38b.7-40a.5 (chapter 33, nges pa'i lung dang drang ba'i lung)

paraphrase: Definitive and provisional teaching: resting in the nature beyond conceptual examination — not meditating on samādhi, without a mind of desire or a fruit to be taken — one reaches the buddha-ground without travelling a path, finds self-arising wisdom without training awareness, accomplishes activity without seeking, and is naturally pure without guarding samaya; buddhas and beings are not seen as two. That the three-kāya teachers teach separately is a provisional teaching (drang ba'i lung) with respect to suchness.
speaker: the all-creating king, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po)
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked). A text-internal use of the provisional/definitive distinction (cf. principle P5-neyartha).

location.section: D828 ff. 49b.6-50b.6 (chapter 44, rdzogs chen skal med don med kyi le'u)

original.text: de bas rgyu 'bras 'das pa'i rdzogs chen la/ /skal med rnams kyi spyod yul ma yin pas/ /rgyu dang 'bras bu'i chos la spyad par bya/
original.edition: Derge Kangyur (sde dge bka' 'gyur), digital edition by Esukhia and Barom Theksum Choling, Tōh 828; Wylie by the unit (pyewts)
original.licence: Public domain (Derge xylograph; Esukhia/Barom digital edition, per the repository)

paraphrase: Nothing to be done: the all-creating king has already accomplished everything, so view need not be meditated, samaya need not be kept, the vidyādhara levels and ten grounds need not be trained, and activity need not be sought. One who, not understanding this, strives and meditates to accomplish it contradicts the meaning beyond cause and effect and is seized by the sickness of effort. Therefore, since the Great Perfection beyond cause and effect is not the domain of those without the fortune for it, they should practise the dharma of cause and result.
speaker: the all-creating king, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po)
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

location.section: D828 ff. 50b.6-52b.1 (chapter 45, lta bsgom med kyi le'u)

paraphrase: Without view or meditation: whatever is meditated is my sickness; since bodhicitta, the heart of all, is free of grasped and grasper, there is not an atom to meditate on; as meditating has not produced the fruit for those above, I do not teach that I am attained by meditation. 'Byang' has nothing to be grasped, 'chub' is the heart of all pervading all, 'sems' is self-arising wisdom everywhere.
speaker: the all-creating king, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po)
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

location.section: D828 ff. 52b.1-54a.1 (chapter 46, dam tshig bsrung du med pa'i le'u)

paraphrase: No samaya to guard: for yogins who rely on the cause-and-result scriptures of the three teachers, the two truths and the four valid means are needed; but since the all-creator made all phenomena and made them all bodhicitta, what it made needs no two truths — in bodhicitta there is neither ultimate nor conventional.
speaker: the all-creating king, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po)
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

location.section: D828 ff. 84b.2-85a.6 (chapter 83, bstan pa gang la gzhag pa'i le'u)

paraphrase: To whom the teaching is to be given: not to unfit vessels — those who delight in fame and worldly concerns, are proud, do not honour the excellent, are fickle, lack generosity and faith, want to force practice on their own terms, or harbour harmful intent; from them it is to be kept supremely secret. Signs and faith are first examined; the teacher takes the disciple's body and possessions so as to cut worldly attachment and test the mind-stream; to those who bear the signs, the essence, the all-creating king, is given. Teaching it to the wrong person brings untimely death and fear to both and the decline of the vehicle of the essence.
speaker: the all-creating king, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems kun byed rgyal po)
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

location.section: D832 ff. 110b.1-111b.4 (chapter 1, gleng gzhi'i le'u)

paraphrase: The setting: the Bhagavat, the great enjoyment body, whose nature is the vajra body, speech and mind of all the tathāgatas of the ten directions and four times, abides in Akaniṣṭha in a boundless palace of blazing wisdom-jewels; around him are the tathāgatas named the king of consciousness, the king of form, the king of feeling, the king of perception and so on — the aggregates themselves as the buddhas.
speaker: the tantra's narrator
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

location.section: D832 f. 112a.3-6 (chapter 2)

original.text: e ma'o ngo mtshar rmad kyi chos/ /rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas kun gyi gsang / /skye ba med las thams cad skye/ /skyes pa nyid na'ang skye ba med/

paraphrase: The generation of the primordially enlightened mind as wisdom: 'E ma'o! This wondrous, marvellous dharma, the secret of all perfect buddhas: from the unborn all is born, and in being born there is no birth.' The same is said of ceasing, abiding, objects of observation, and coming and going: from what does not cease, abide, observe or come and go, everything ceases, abides, is observed, comes and goes — and in doing so does not.
speaker: the great being of non-duality (gnyis su med pa'i bdag nyid chen po)
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

location.section: D832 f. 112b.1-4 (chapter 2)

original.text: sus kyang ma bcings bcings med de/ /bcing bar bya ba yod ma yin/ /rnam rtog bdag tu 'dzin pa yis/ /nan gyis mkha' la mdud pa dor/
original.edition: Derge Kangyur (sde dge bka' 'gyur), digital edition by Esukhia and Barom Theksum Choling, Tōh 832; Wylie by the unit (pyewts)
original.licence: Public domain (Derge xylograph; Esukhia/Barom digital edition, per the repository)

paraphrase: Out of great compassion, since beings, though of one nature with the buddhas, wander through the five classes by the conceptuality of ignorance: 'E ma! From the sugata-essence, by one's own conceptual karma are emanated bodies, enjoyments, abodes, sufferings and the rest, and one grasps them as I and mine. No one binds; there is no bondage and nothing to be bound. Grasping a self through conceptuality, one forcibly ties knots in space. The buddha-dharma, spontaneously perfect from the beginning, without bondage or liberation, displays varied activity in order to be taught.'
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

location.section: D832 f. 113a.1-7 (chapter 3, chos thams cad gtan la phab pa)

paraphrase: The six sages emanated from the buddhas' body, speech and mind teach, according to those to be tamed, the vehicles of gods and humans, of śrāvakas, of pratyekabuddhas, of bodhisattvas and the unsurpassed vehicle: eighty-four thousand teachings as antidotes to the eighty-four thousand afflictions arising from ignorant conceptuality. All of them show that grasped and grasper arise interdependently, that karma and its result are not wasted, and ultimately that one is not stained by karma and its result.
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The samaya chapter closes: for the faithful who enter the maṇḍala of great bliss and keep the samaya, the wisdom of equal fortune arises when sought and great wonder is certain; one without faith who breaks it is ruined.

location.section: D832 ff. 124a.1-124b.3 (chapter 13, shin tu gsang ba man ngag gi le'u)

paraphrase: The most secret instruction: the maṇḍala of Samantabhadra, gazed upon by the five wisdoms, is spontaneously perfect; this is the great secret fruit taken as the path, by which the five kāyas are spontaneously perfected — there is no more secret definitive meaning in all the victors' maṇḍalas. It is to be given only to those with the eye of wisdom trained in hearing, reflection and meditation, fit vessels of good character who offer body and wealth — never otherwise; if it is proclaimed to the deluded, their life ends untimely and they remain long burning and scorched.
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked). Chapter 13 is the chapter on which the Garland of Views (src:mengak-tawai-trengwa) comments.

original.edition: Derge Tengyur (sde dge bstan 'gyur), digital edition by Esukhia and Barom Theksum Choling, Tōh 2591; Wylie by the unit (pyewts)

paraphrase: This path of the great sage is subtle and hard to know: non-conceptual, beyond conceptions, hard to examine and to teach, free of verbal convention and not within the reach of the immature — one looks to the Teacher's definitive scripture and the instructions of holy masters. Analysis that takes perception and the like as valid means follows an endless stream of conceptions and cannot reach the essence; therefore the worldly conventions of examination are not needed on this yogic path.
speaker: Mañjuśrīmitra
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Those deceived by conceptions, following the stream of delusion like dreamers taking dreams as true, who abandon this path and teach other paths as the unmistaken one, are like gold in ore — worthy of compassion. May this unsurpassed non-dual path, established by valid means through the power of familiarity, spread for the benefit of beings.
speaker: Mañjuśrīmitra
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked). The phrase 'rdo la gser bzhin' (like gold in ore) gives the text its Tibetan name.

paraphrase: First statement: introduce (the disciple) directly to their own nature — awareness is pointed out face to face.
speaker: Garab Dorje

original.edition: as commonly recited; transcription by the unit

paraphrase: Second statement: decide on one thing — settle with certainty that there is nothing other than this awareness.
speaker: Garab Dorje
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

original.edition: as commonly recited; transcription by the unit

paraphrase: Third statement: gain confidence directly in liberation — whatever arises is liberated in awareness itself, and one is confident in this self-liberation.
speaker: Garab Dorje
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Four ways of leaving things as they are: the view like a mountain (unmoved), meditation like the ocean (undisturbed), conduct as appearances left as they are, and the fruit as awareness left as it is.
speaker: Jñānasūtra
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The Cuckoo of Awareness: the nature of variety is non-dual; each thing is free of elaboration; though not conceived as 'suchness', the all-good appears everywhere; being already complete, give up the sickness of effort; remaining spontaneously is the settling.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). Wording checked through its occurrence as chapter 31 of the local Kunjed Gyalpo.

paraphrase: Patrul Rinpoche opens by naming the lineage in terms of the path: the view is Longchen Rabjam (vast expanse), the meditation is Khyentse Özer (rays of wisdom and love), the conduct is Gyalwai Nyugu (the victors' offspring) — whoever practises thus attains buddhahood without effort.
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Commenting on the three statements: relax body and mind, then with a sudden forceful 'phaṭ' cut through thought; in the startled openness awareness is naked — this is the introduction; decide there is nothing else; and let thoughts arising be liberated as they arise, like drawings on water, so that meditation and post-meditation are not divided.
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: All things of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa have one ground, two paths and two results — the magical display of awareness and of ignorance. By Samantabhadra's aspiration may all beings recognize the ground and attain perfect buddhahood in the palace of the dharmadhātu.
speaker: Samantabhadra
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Samantabhadra's account of his own liberation: the ground is uncompounded, self-arisen, inexpressible, beyond saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; recognizing it, one is buddha; not recognizing it, beings wander. He, Samantabhadra, recognized that ground-appearances are his own display and so, without having done a single virtue, was liberated; for beings who did not recognize, ignorance arose as a blank unawareness and a conceptual ignorance, and from them saṃsāra.
speaker: Samantabhadra
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The aspiration then takes up each afflictive state — desire, anger, pride, jealousy and dullness — describing the realm into which it leads, and prays that, by relaxing into the natural state without grasping or rejecting, each be recognized and liberated as its wisdom.
speaker: Samantabhadra
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

original.text: hUM/ o rgyan yul gyi nub byang mtshams/ /padma ge sar sdong po la/ /ya mtshan mchog gi dngos grub brnyes/ /padma 'byung gnas zhes su grags/ /'khor du mkha' 'gro mang pos bskor/ /khyed kyi rjes su bdag bsgrub kyis/ /byin gyis rlob phyir gshegs su gsol/ gu ru padma siddhi hUM/
original.edition: as commonly recited; transcription by the unit

paraphrase: Hūṃ. On the north-west border of the land of Oḍḍiyāna, on the pistil-stem of a lotus, you attained the marvellous supreme siddhi; renowned as the Lotus-born, surrounded by a retinue of many ḍākinīs: following you I practise; come, I pray, to grant your blessing. Guru padma siddhi hūṃ.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Padmasambhava is born, without father or mother, from a lotus on Lake Dhanakośa in Oḍḍiyāna as an emanation of Amitābha; the childless King Indrabhūti finds him and adopts him as prince.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). Chapter-level locator not recorded.

paraphrase: Invited by Trisong Detsen on Śāntarakṣita's advice, Padmasambhava binds under oath the gods and spirits of Tibet who were obstructing the work, so that Samye can be built and consecrated.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Before leaving Tibet Padmasambhava gives prophecies and final advice, conceals teachings as treasures for future times, and departs on a horse through the sky to the south-west land of the rākṣasas to subdue them.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The Testament of Ba reports that under Trisong Detsen the followers of the Chinese master Moheyan, teaching sudden non-conceptuality, and the Indian party led by Kamalaśīla, teaching the gradual path of the perfections, debated before the king, who ruled that Tibetans should follow Nāgārjuna's view and the gradual path (tradition's account).
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The Garland of Views ranks views from the lowest up: worldly people without a view of karma, non-Buddhist eternalists and nihilists, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas; then the outer tantras (kriyā, ubhaya, yoga); then the inner: Mahāyoga's generation, Anuyoga's completion and Atiyoga's Great Perfection — each higher view including what the lower sought.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: In the Great Perfection all phenomena of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are realized to have been enlightened from the beginning as the nature of the maṇḍala of body, speech and mind, so that there is nothing to be sought or accomplished; this realization, not a meditation that produces it, is the view of Atiyoga.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Nupchen presents the gradual approach (rim gyis pa) taught by Kamalaśīla — calm and analytical insight cultivated step by step — as authentic but the lowest of the four approaches he compares.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). Section-level locator; chapter numbers not recorded.

paraphrase: The simultaneous approach (cig car ba) of the Chan master Moheyan — entering non-conceptuality directly without gradual steps — is presented with respect as higher than the gradual, yet below Mahāyoga and the Great Perfection.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The Great Perfection is distinguished from the simultaneous approach: it does not rely on the effort of fixing on non-conceptuality but on the primordially present great self-arising wisdom in which there is nothing to cultivate or reject — so Atiyoga is placed highest.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Rongzom argues that all appearances are established only as appearances, like illusions, and that the Great Perfection's claim that all is primordially enlightened does not deny appearance but recognizes it as pure from the beginning; errors come from taking appearances as real.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Rongzom reads the Guhyagarbha as teaching the great purity of all phenomena as the deities and their great equality in emptiness, so that the maṇḍala is not imagined but is how things are.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Longchenpa sings of the dharmadhātu as the primordial expanse: all phenomena of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa arise within it as its display, like the sky's contents within the sky, uncreated and unchanging; the mind that realizes this has nothing to add or remove.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). Chapter-level; the chapter division of the Chöying Dzöd (13 chapters) is from memory.

paraphrase: The first vajra topic, the ground: its essence is primordially pure, its nature spontaneously present, its compassion all-pervading; it is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa and is described as a youthful vase body — luminosity enclosed within.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: How delusion arises: when the ground-appearances emerge from the ground through the eight gateways of spontaneous presence, not recognizing them as one's own display is ignorance (in three kinds), and the dualistic apprehension of self and other unfolds into the realms of saṃsāra.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The abode of wisdom in the body: wisdom dwells in the heart (the precious citta palace) as the luminous essence, connects through the crystal kati channel to the eyes, and manifests through the lamps (sgron ma); the channels, winds and essences are the body's support of the path.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). Topic numbers 3-5 approximate. Doctrinal anatomy only; the practices built on it are restricted (prc:togal).

paraphrase: Cutting through (khregs chod) releases the practitioner into primordial purity and suits those who prefer ease; direct crossing (thod rgal) brings spontaneous presence to manifestation through the four visions and suits the diligent; the first frees the mind, the second also exhausts the body's elements into light.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). Summary of a well-known Nyingthig distinction; exact locus in the Tegchok Dzöd not recorded. Tögal content restricted: no method recorded.

paraphrase: The four samayas of the Great Perfection: non-existence (med pa: nothing is established), evenness or all-pervasiveness (phyal ba: all is equal in the expanse), spontaneous presence (lhun grub: everything is already accomplished) and singularity (gcig pu: all is one in the nature of mind) — kept by realizing them, not by rules.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Longchenpa's doxography concludes with the Great Perfection as the summit of the nine vehicles, in which the lower vehicles' views are included and surpassed.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Finding Rest in the Nature of Mind opens with the rarity of the human existence endowed with the eight freedoms and ten advantages and urges using it for the Dharma.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The place for meditation: a solitary, pleasant place suited to the season and to one's practice — high and open for clarity, enclosed for calm — free of dangers and disturbances.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The person who meditates: one with renunciation, faith and diligence, who has turned from worldly concerns, keeps the vows and relies on a qualified teacher.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The practice: preliminaries, then the main meditations that bring the experiences of bliss, clarity and non-thought, each to be released without attachment lest it lead into the desire, form or formless realms; then non-conceptual wisdom.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: All phenomena are to be understood as illusion through eight similes — dream, magic show, optical illusion, mirage, echo, city of gandharvas, reflection and emanation — so that clinging to their reality relaxes and one finds rest.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The extraordinary preliminaries: the practices of separating saṃsāra from nirvāṇa (ru shan) through body, speech and mind — exhausting ordinary activity, training with the syllable hūṃ, and searching for where mind comes from, stays and goes — so that one does not mistake ordinary mind for awareness.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Cutting through: after the introduction by the master, awareness is recognized as fresh, naked and unfabricated; one rests in it without meditating, and whatever arises is liberated by itself; the faults of stupor, agitation and fabrication are recognized and left.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Direct crossing is taught only to those stable in cutting through: relying on the key points given orally by the master, the lamps bring forth the four visions, culminating in the exhaustion of phenomena in dharmatā. The text insists that the instructions be received from a qualified master and practised under guidance.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). RESTRICTED: summary and the text's own warning only; no method recorded.

paraphrase: Instructions for those not liberated in life: at death recognize the ground luminosity (the meeting of mother and child luminosity); failing that, recognize the lights and deities of the bardo of dharmatā as one's own display; failing that, take a birth in a pure land through the bardo of becoming.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Jigme Lingpa's Treasury of Precious Qualities begins with the freedoms and advantages and the thoughts that turn the mind, then proceeds through the vehicles to the Great Perfection.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: At the end of guru yoga the practitioner receives the four empowerments: from the guru's forehead (oṃ) white light purifies the body and gives the vase empowerment; from the throat (āḥ) red light purifies speech and gives the secret empowerment; from the heart (hūṃ) blue light purifies mind and gives the wisdom empowerment; and from all three the fourth, the word empowerment; then guru and disciple mingle and one rests in the nature of mind.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: How to listen: avoid the three defects of the vessel (an upturned pot that hears nothing, a leaking pot that forgets, a pot with poison that mixes the teaching with bad motives) and the six stains (pride, lack of faith, lack of interest, outward distraction, inward tension, weariness); listen with the vast attitude of bodhicitta and the skilful attitude of secret mantra, seeing teacher, place and teaching as pure.
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche (recording Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The difficulty of finding the freedoms and advantages: a human life free of the eight unfree states and endowed with the ten advantages (five personal, five circumstantial) is rarer than a turtle putting its head through a yoke on the ocean; it is also threatened by the eight intrusive circumstances and eight incompatible propensities.
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche (recording Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The impermanence of life: the outer universe, the beings in it, even holy beings and the buddhas pass away; the circumstances of death are countless and the time uncertain; so one should practise now.
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche (recording Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The defects of saṃsāra: the sufferings of the hells, the hungry spirits, the animals, humans (birth, ageing, sickness, death and more), the demigods and the gods — there is no place in saṃsāra beyond suffering.
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche (recording Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Actions, cause and effect: the ten non-virtuous actions and their fully ripened effect, the effect similar to the cause (in experience and in tendency) and the conditioning effect; the ten virtues to be adopted; the smallest act is not wasted.
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche (recording Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The benefits of liberation: only liberation and omniscience are free of suffering; the aspiration for them is roused by the preceding contemplations.
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche (recording Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: How to follow a spiritual teacher: examine the teacher first (pure vows, learning, compassion, experience of the practice, freedom from worldly aims), rather than taking anyone because of fame; then follow him with faith and service, and emulate his realization and conduct; false teachers are compared to a millstone tied around the neck.
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche (recording Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Taking refuge: the refuge of faith in the Three Jewels, and in the Three Roots (guru, yidam, ḍākinī) and in the channels, winds and essences and the nature of mind, visualized as the refuge tree; with prostrations; and the precepts of refuge (what to avoid, what to do, and additional practices).
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche (recording Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Arousing bodhicitta: training in the four boundless attitudes, then the aspiring and applying bodhicitta, equalizing and exchanging oneself and others and taking on others' suffering; the precepts of the bodhisattva.
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche (recording Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Meditation and recitation of Vajrasattva to purify wrongdoing and obscurations, complete with the four powers: the power of the support, of regret, of resolution, and of the antidote (the visualization and the hundred-syllable mantra).
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche (recording Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The maṇḍala offering to gather the two accumulations of merit and wisdom: offering the universe and all one's wealth and merit to the Three Jewels.
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche (recording Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The kusāli's accumulation: the renunciant's offering of his own body, visualized as cut up and transformed into nectar for the guests of the four kinds, cutting attachment to the body.
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche (recording Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Guru yoga, the ultimate method for arousing wisdom: visualizing the guru as Padmasambhava, supplicating him with the Seven-line prayer and the Vajra Guru mantra, receiving the four empowerments and mixing one's mind with his; devotion is said to be the only cause of the realization of the natural state.
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche (recording Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Transference of consciousness (phowa), 'buddhahood without meditation', is taught as an auxiliary. Of its kinds (dharmakāya, sambhogakāya, nirmāṇakāya, the ordinary transference with three recognitions, and the transference for the dead by the hook of compassion), only the ordinary one is practised in training, and never applied before the signs of death are complete: to transfer untimely is like killing the deities.
speaker: Patrul Rinpoche (recording Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). RESTRICTED: classification and the text's warning only; no method recorded.

paraphrase: At the moment of death the dying person is called by name and introduced to the clear light: 'O noble one, what is called death has now come; the luminosity of dharmatā is dawning — recognize it as your own awareness, empty and luminous, and rest in it'; recognition at this point is liberation.
speaker: the reader (lama)
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: In the bardo of dharmatā the peaceful deities appear day by day — the five buddhas with their consorts, the bodhisattvas and the rest — radiating brilliant wisdom lights, while dull lights of the six realms appear beside them; the deceased is urged not to fear the brilliant lights nor to be drawn to the dull ones, and to recognize everything as the display of their own awareness.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Later the wrathful deities — the herukas with their consorts, the gaurīs, piśācīs, gatekeepers and īśvarīs — appear in terrifying forms; they are the same deities in wrathful aspect, and recognizing them as one's own projections liberates.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: In the bardo of becoming the deceased has a mental body driven by karma, sees the Lord of Death weigh deeds in the mirror of karma, and is urged to close the womb door by the methods taught or, failing that, to choose a favourable birth or a pure land.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The text is to be read aloud to the dying and dead over the forty-nine days; merely hearing it, the tradition says, can liberate even without meditation, and it should also be studied in life.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The root verses exhort the practitioner in each intermediate state: in the bardo of life, give up laziness and enter hearing, reflection and meditation; in the bardo of dream, give up the corpse-like sleep of ignorance and recognize the dream; in the bardo of meditation, rest undistracted; in the bardo of dying, give up clinging and enter the clear light; in the bardo of dharmatā, recognize the appearances as self-display; in the bardo of becoming, close the womb door and remember pure perception.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Karma Lingpa's text teaches how to examine the outer, inner and secret signs of approaching death and, where they appear before one's time, the rites that ransom and avert death; when death is certain, one prepares with transference and the bardo instructions.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Whether the ultimate is an affirming or non-affirming negation: for the provisional, enumerated ultimate the emptiness that negates true existence is a non-affirming negation; the actual ultimate, realized in meditative equipoise, is the union of appearance and emptiness beyond all four extremes — neither kind of negation.
speaker: Mipham
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Whether to analyse or to rest: analytical meditation produces certainty, and resting meditation lets that certainty settle without concepts; the two are to be alternated, the analysis of the paṇḍita and the resting of the kusāli supporting one another.
speaker: Mipham
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Whether Madhyamaka has a thesis: from the standpoint of the ultimate free of extremes, there is no thesis to hold; conventionally, the Mādhyamika asserts, teaches and refutes.
speaker: Mipham
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Buddha-nature is the union of luminosity and emptiness: its emptiness keeps it from being an existent self, its luminosity means the buddha-qualities are primordially present rather than newly produced; to take it as a mere absence or as a permanent entity are both errors.
speaker: Mipham
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Mipham's overview of the Guhyagarbha: all phenomena are great purity — appearances are the deities and pure lands — and great equality — they are empty; the inseparability of the two is the 'superior two truths' of Mahāyoga, established by the pure-vision valid cognition.
speaker: Mipham
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: In the wisdom chapter commentary Mipham holds that Prāsaṅgika analysis negates all extremes without leaving a qualified remainder, so that in equipoise nothing — not even emptiness — is grasped; Gelug scholars answered that this blurs the object of negation.
speaker: Mipham
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Dudjom Rinpoche sets out the nine vehicles in three triads: the vehicles that lead out from the origin of suffering (śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva); the vehicles of Vedic austerity (kriyā, ubhaya/caryā, yoga); and the vehicles of overpowering means (mahāyoga, anuyoga, atiyoga).
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: Treasure teachings pass through the three common transmissions (the victors' mind-transmission, the vidyādharas' symbolic transmission, the oral transmission of persons) and three special ones (prophetic authorization, empowerment through aspiration, entrustment to the ḍākinīs), and are revealed by the treasure revealer at the destined time.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The ground's display arises as sound, light and rays (sgra 'od zer gsum); recognizing them as one's own display is liberation, taking them as other is the root of delusion.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). Locus within the tantra not recorded.

paraphrase: The tantra describes the outer signs at the death of accomplished practitioners — relics of various kinds, lights, sounds and earth tremors — as marks of the degree of realization.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase).

paraphrase: The nine ways of Bön: four causal ways — of prediction (phywa gshen), of the visible world (snang gshen), of magical power ('phrul gshen) and of existence (srid gshen) — and five fruitional ways — of lay followers (dge bsnyen), of ascetics (drang srong), of the white A (a dkar), of the primordial shen (ye gshen) and the unsurpassed way (bla med, Dzogchen).
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). Optional (Bön). Section-level reference from general knowledge.

paraphrase: Tönpa Shenrab pursues into Tibet the demon Khyapa Lagring, who had stolen his horses; in Kongpo he teaches the Tibetans rites of offering and purification, and eventually converts the demon.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). Optional (Bön). Section-level reference from general knowledge.

paraphrase: The general view: the base of all (kun gzhi) is empty and clear; awareness (rig pa) is inseparable from it; their inseparability is the natural state, uncreated and without deviation.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). Optional (Bön). Section-level reference from general knowledge.

paraphrase: Seeing awareness nakedly: the master introduces the disciple to naked awareness beyond the conceptual mind, likened to the sky, the sun and its rays; one then rests in it without correction.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). Optional (Bön). Section-level reference from general knowledge.

paraphrase: Tapihritsa, appearing as a boy, questions the learned Gyerpung Nangzher Löpo and shows him that his pride in scholarship and powers obstructs the natural state, then transmits the teaching that became the Oral Transmission.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). Optional (Bön). Section-level reference from general knowledge.

paraphrase: The A-tri begins calm abiding by fixing the mind on a white letter A (within a sphere of light), then dissolving the support and resting without support in the natural state, and finally integrating that state with activity.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). Optional (Bön). Section-level reference from general knowledge.

paraphrase: Shardza's history traces Bön from Tönpa Shenrab in Ölmo Lungring to Zhang Zhung and Tibet, through persecutions (under Drigum Tsenpo and under Trisong Detsen) when texts were hidden, to their recovery as treasures and the founding of the monastic seats.
notes: Reference from the unit author's knowledge (not read in a local text in this phase). Optional (Bön). From general knowledge.

paraphrase: The wheel of the garland of syllables: without moving from the samādhi in which all phenomena are primordially enlightened, the tathāgatas bring forth the syllables in which all phenomena abide as mere names. From the stable white A, extremely subtle A's radiate, filling the ten directions, and are gathered without increase or decrease; from them all groups of names blaze forth and are gathered — the cause of the stable wisdom of vajra accomplishment. The alphabet is uttered, the six worlds quake, and all phenomena become mere marks of names. 'A is neither empty nor not empty, and no middle is found either; all buddhas, mere names, abide in the garland of syllables; A itself appears as the variety, ka and the rest.'
notes: Passage located and read in the local Derge e-text (folio in location.section); paraphrase by U45 from the Tibetan (skeleton phase, fidelity not yet checked). The link to the Dzogchen 'sound, light and rays' concept is thematic (sound as display), added by the unit.
